title: The Rider and the Elephant
book: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion
author: Jonathan Haidt
wiifm: Every time you try to persuade a client, a regulator, a colleague or your partner, you run into the fact that people decide first and reason second. The Righteous Mind explains why, and why decent people end up in furious disagreement. You will follow Jonathan Haidt from a liberal Jewish upbringing in New York to a village in India that rearranged his view of morality, and then into the laboratory where he asked people whether it was wrong to eat the family dog. You will leave knowing how to talk to the elephant, not just the rider.

b: Jonathan David Haidt was born on the nineteenth of October 1963 in New York City and grew up in Scarsdale, a comfortable suburb north of the city. His family was Jewish and politically liberal, and he has written that he absorbed the assumptions of that world without questioning them: that conservatives were mostly wrong, and possibly a bit wicked.

He went to Yale and studied philosophy, graduating in 1985. Philosophy taught him to ask what morality is, but it seemed to assume that moral judgements come mainly from careful reasoning. Haidt was not so sure. He was drawn instead to psychology, to how real people actually make moral judgements, and he took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania, completing it in 1992.

At Penn he worked alongside the psychologist Paul Rozin, a pioneer in the study of disgust, the emotion that makes us recoil from rotten food and, it turns out, from certain kinds of people and acts. Disgust became a key to Haidt's thinking. It was fast, physical and hard to argue with, and it seemed to play a far larger role in moral life than philosophers had admitted.

Keep the young Haidt in mind, a clever liberal who thought he knew who was right. The whole book is the story of how he was gradually forced to change his mind, and what he learned about minds in the process.

At the time, moral psychology was dominated by the work of Lawrence Kohlberg, who described children climbing a ladder of ever more sophisticated moral reasoning, with abstract justice at the top. In that picture, morality was mainly something you worked out in your head. Haidt suspected the head was arriving late to a decision that had already been made somewhere else.
ch.cap: Young Haidt doubts the ladder of moral reasoning

b: At Penn, Haidt designed a now-famous set of stories. A family's dog is killed by a car outside their house. They have heard dog meat is delicious, so they cook it and eat it for dinner. Nobody sees. A man buys a chicken from the supermarket and does something sexual with it before cooking and eating it. A woman cleans her toilet with an old national flag.

Nobody is harmed in any of these stories. Yet most people Haidt interviewed said they were wrong. When he pressed them for reasons, they reached for harms that were not there: someone might see, the person might get ill. When he pointed out that the story ruled those out, many people still insisted it was wrong, and could only say something like I know it is wrong, I just cannot explain why. Haidt called this moral dumbfounding.

Importantly, the pattern varied. In a 1993 study across cities in the United States and Brazil, wealthier, more educated Westerners were most likely to say harmless acts were fine. Working class people, and Brazilians, were more likely to condemn them. Morality, it seemed, was wider than harm in most of the world.

One of the stories involved an adult brother and sister on holiday who decide, once, to sleep together, using two forms of contraception, and agree never to do it again. Nobody is harmed and nobody finds out. Almost everyone says it is wrong, and almost nobody can explain why in terms of harm. That story, more than any other, became the emblem of moral dumbfounding.
ch.cap: A dumbfounded subject can't say why it's wrong

b: In 1993 Haidt spent three months in Bhubaneswar, in the Indian state of Orissa, now Odisha, working with the anthropologist Richard Shweder, who had argued that Western morality was unusually narrow. Haidt lived in a world where men and women were often separated, where purity and pollution mattered in daily life, and where elders were addressed with great deference.

At first it felt alien and, to a liberal American, uncomfortable. But over the weeks something shifted. He began to see a moral world in which duty, respect and sanctity held a society together, and he found he could appreciate it from the inside. He has written that he came home able to see a broader moral landscape, and with a new curiosity about American conservatives, whose concerns with loyalty, authority and sanctity suddenly looked less like mere prejudice.

That trip planted the seeds of the book. Haidt taught at the University of Virginia from 1995, and later moved to New York University's Stern School of Business. He published The Righteous Mind in 2012.

He has described one moment in particular. Dining with men whose wives silently served the food and then withdrew to the kitchen, he found that his liberal reflexes protested, yet the people around him plainly felt that they were part of a moral order that gave everyone a place. He did not abandon his own values. He simply stopped assuming they were the only ones a decent person could hold.

The experience also taught him something about method. Rather than asking people to reason their way to a moral principle, he began to watch what they actually felt and did, and to treat their gut reactions as data worth explaining rather than errors to be corrected. That shift, from the philosophy seminar to the field, runs through the whole book.
ch.cap: Haidt dines in Bhubaneswar while the women serve

b: The book's first principle is that intuitions come first, and strategic reasoning second. Haidt's image for this is a small rider sitting on a large elephant. The elephant is our intuition, our fast, automatic, emotional response. The rider is conscious reasoning. We like to think the rider is in charge. Most of the time, Haidt argues, the rider is more like a press secretary, whose job is to explain and justify whatever the elephant has already decided.

He draws on research such as Michael Gazzaniga's work with split-brain patients, whose speaking hemisphere confidently invented reasons for actions it had not chosen, and on studies of how people search for evidence that supports what they already believe. We reason, he argues, less like scientists searching for truth and more like lawyers defending a client.

The metaphor first appeared in his earlier book, The Happiness Hypothesis, in 2006. In The Righteous Mind he adds a story from Plato's Republic. Glaucon, Socrates's companion, asks whether a man who owned a ring of invisibility, and could never be caught, would still behave justly. Haidt says Glaucon was on to something: people care more about looking good than being good. Our reasoning is designed less to find truth than to protect our reputation in the eyes of others.

The practical lesson is enormous. If you want to change someone's mind, arguments alone rarely work. You have to speak to the elephant: through relationships, respect, stories and feelings, so that the person's intuitions begin to lean your way. Then the rider will happily find the reasons.
ch.cap: A tiny rider explains where the elephant goes

b: The second principle is that there is more to morality than harm and fairness. Haidt compares morality to the tongue. Just as the tongue has different taste receptors, sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savoury, the moral mind has several foundations, each tuned to a challenge our ancestors faced. With Craig Joseph, Jesse Graham and others he developed what he called Moral Foundations Theory.

In the book there are six. Care and harm, rooted in protecting vulnerable children. Fairness and cheating, rooted in reciprocal cooperation. Loyalty and betrayal, rooted in holding groups together. Authority and subversion, rooted in managing hierarchies. Sanctity and degradation, rooted in avoiding disease and contamination, and later extended to the sense that some things are sacred. And liberty and oppression, added in the book, rooted in resistance to bullies and tyrants.

The crucial finding came from surveys of many thousands of people on his website. Liberals, in the American sense of the word, relied heavily on care and fairness, and somewhat on liberty. Conservatives used all of the foundations more evenly. In Haidt's metaphor, liberals have a two or three receptor morality. Conservatives have a broader palate, and that, he argued, gives them an advantage in speaking to voters.

Haidt also noticed that even shared foundations could mean different things. Both sides care about fairness, but liberals tend to mean equality, everyone getting the same, while conservatives tend to mean proportionality, people getting what they deserve, with cheats and free riders punished. Many arguments about welfare or taxes, he suggests, are really arguments between these two flavours of fairness.
ch.cap: Six moral flavours wait on the tasting table

ch.h: Ninety per cent chimp, ten per cent bee
b: The third principle is that morality binds and blinds. Here Haidt turns to evolution. He accepts that much of human nature is selfish, shaped by competition between individuals. But he argues, controversially, that humans also evolved in competition between groups, and that groups with members who could pull together, sacrifice for each other and suppress cheating tended to win.

His phrase for the result is that we are ninety per cent chimp and ten per cent bee. Mostly we are self-interested primates. But under the right conditions, in collective rituals, shared danger, sport or worship, we can flip a switch that he calls the hive switch, losing ourselves in something bigger. He suggests this is part of why religion is so universal: it binds people into moral communities, though he notes it also blinds them to the views of outsiders.

He borrows from the French sociologist Emile Durkheim, who wrote about the collective effervescence people feel at festivals and ceremonies, and from the historian William McNeill, who described the strange bond produced by soldiers drilling in step. Haidt suggests leaders can use the same psychology at work, by making people feel part of a team with a shared mission rather than a collection of individuals with contracts.

This part of the book leans on multilevel selection, the idea that natural selection can act on groups as well as individuals. Many evolutionary biologists, including Steven Pinker and others in the tradition Dawkins described, are sceptical of group selection. So treat the evolutionary story as a hypothesis, while noting that the psychology of the hive, the joy of belonging and the blindness that comes with it, is easy to recognise.
ch.cap: Drilling soldiers flip the hive switch as one

b: Put the three principles together and you get Haidt's answer to his subtitle. Good people are divided by politics and religion because each side's elephant responds to a different set of moral tastes, each side's rider is busy justifying its elephant, and each side is bound into a team that blinds it to the other.

Haidt has a striking test. He asked liberals and conservatives to fill in a questionnaire as they thought a typical person on the other side would. Conservatives and moderates predicted liberal answers fairly well. Liberals were worst at predicting conservative answers, especially on care and fairness, where they assumed conservatives did not care about harm at all. Haidt, himself a liberal by background, found this humbling.

He does not conclude that one side is right. He argues that liberals are better at seeing victims and pushing for change, while conservatives are better at seeing what holds a society together, and that a healthy country needs both. He described himself after writing the book as a centrist.

He calls each side's shared set of values a moral matrix, borrowing from the film The Matrix. Inside your own matrix, your values look like simple common sense, and those of the other side look absurd. Stepping outside, even briefly, is uncomfortable, but it is the only way to understand why your opponents feel as strongly as you do.

He also suggests that the left and the right each hold part of the truth about a society's ecosystem. In his memorable comparison, conservatives guard the moral capital of a community, the habits and institutions built up over generations, while liberals keep it honest by spotting who is being harmed or excluded. Lose either, he argues, and the community suffers.
ch.cap: Two riders on rival elephants face off

b: The Righteous Mind has been widely praised and seriously criticised. Some psychologists argue that reasoning matters more than Haidt allows, pointing to studies where people do change their moral views after reflection and argument over time. The philosopher Paul Bloom, among others, has made this case.

Moral Foundations Theory has also been challenged. Some researchers, such as Kurt Gray, argue that most moral judgements reduce to perceptions of harm, even in apparently harmless cases, because people imagine victims. Others have questioned whether the foundations are truly distinct, whether the questionnaire measures them reliably across cultures, and whether the liberal and conservative differences are as clean outside the United States. And as we have seen, the group selection story remains contested.

Most readers come away with a version that survives these challenges: intuition leads, reasoning follows more often than we like to admit, and people in different camps care about genuinely different things, not simply about the same things more or less.

He also draws on the observation, by Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan in 2010, that most psychology studies use people who are Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic, a group they called WEIRD. Such people are unusual by world standards, more individualistic and more focused on harm and rights. Haidt's warning is that a morality built only on WEIRD intuitions misses much of humanity.
ch.cap: A WEIRD student sits in the spotlight; humanity waits

b: Haidt went on to co-write The Coddling of the American Mind with Greg Lukianoff in 2018, and The Anxious Generation in 2024, about smartphones and young people's mental health, which has attracted its own fierce debate. But The Righteous Mind remains his foundational work.

In 2015 he co-founded Heterodox Academy, a group encouraging a wider range of viewpoints in universities, a practical expression of the book's argument that people reason better when someone in the room disagrees with them.

Its lesson for daily life is gentle and practical. When you disagree with someone, assume first that they are not stupid or evil but tasting a different moral flavour. Find something you genuinely respect in their view. Build a relationship before you build an argument. Speak to their elephant, and then, often, their rider will follow.

Haidt's own journey is the best illustration of the book. He started as a liberal who thought conservatives were mostly wrong. He spent years studying their intuitions, and came out not as a convert but as someone who could see why decent people disagree. The point was never to make everyone agree. It was to make disagreement less poisonous.
ch.cap: Haidt speaks gently to another person's elephant

take: People decide by intuition and then justify. Build trust, warmth and a clear story before you present the facts, whether you are selling or negotiating.
Reasons offered for a decision are often after the fact. Watch what people do and feel, not only what they say.
Messages that touch loyalty, respect and integrity as well as care and fairness reach a wider audience. Tailor the value, not just the facts.
Most disagreement comes from different moral tastes, not malice. Start by naming something you respect in the other side's view.
Liberals in Haidt's study misread conservatives most. Try describing a rival's position so well they would agree with your summary.
Shared rituals and goals make people pull together. Celebrate team wins and shared purpose to bind staff, while staying open to outsiders.
Arguments rarely win in the moment. Let people reflect, keep the relationship warm and give them a respectful way to change their view.

stories: The family that ate the dog

At the University of Pennsylvania in the early 1990s, Jonathan Haidt read people a short story. A family's dog is killed by a car outside their house. They have heard dog meat is delicious, so they cook it and eat it. Nobody sees, nobody is harmed. Is it wrong? Most people said yes. Asked why, they invented harms the story had ruled out: someone might find out, they might get ill. When Haidt pointed this out, many still said, in effect, I know it is wrong, I just cannot explain why. He called it moral dumbfounding. The judgement came first, and the reasons were hunted for afterwards.

In 1993 Haidt, a liberal American from a New York suburb, spent three months in Bhubaneswar in eastern India, working with the anthropologist Richard Shweder. He found himself at dinners where the wives silently served the men and withdrew to the kitchen. His liberal reflexes protested. But the people around him clearly felt part of a moral order that gave everyone a place, built on duty, respect and purity. Over the weeks he found he could see that world from the inside. He did not give up his own values. He simply stopped assuming they were the only ones a decent person could hold, and came home curious about conservatives at last.

Haidt ran a simple, humbling test. He asked thousands of liberals and conservatives to fill in his moral questionnaire twice: once as themselves, and once as they thought a typical person on the other side would. You might expect everyone to caricature their opponents equally. They did not. Conservatives and moderates predicted liberal answers fairly well. The liberals, Haidt's own tribe, were worst at predicting conservatives, especially on care and fairness, where many assumed conservatives simply did not care about suffering. The side that prided itself on open-mindedness understood the other side least. Haidt took it as a warning about his own blind spots.
biz: A homeowner decides whether to trust you in the first few seconds, long before they weigh rates and terms, and the rider then finds reasons. Respect that honestly rather than exploiting it. This week, rewrite the first WhatsApp message and the opening of the phone script so they lead with who you are, that you are an FCA-authorised broker and not a lender, what will happen next, and that there is no obligation, with the required warning that their home may be repossessed kept clear. Give people time to think and never push a decision. Measure reply rate to the first message and drop-off before the fact-find.

Haidt shows people respond to different moral tastes: care, fairness, liberty, loyalty, authority. Homeowners looking for a secured loan are not one audience. This month, run a fair test across Google, Bing and Facebook with three honest ad angles, each true and each with the same required risk warning: care, such as improving the family home; liberty, such as understanding all your options before you decide; and authority, such as an FCA-authorised broker working with a panel of lenders. Measure click-through and, more importantly, the share of enquiries that turn out to be suitable. Never use fear, guilt or shame as the hook.
connects: Haidt's elephant and rider is a vivid version of Kahneman's fast intuitive System 1 doing most of the work while slow System 2 justifies it.
Carnegie's advice to avoid arguments and begin with genuine respect is Haidt's speak to the elephant, written seventy years earlier as practical etiquette.
Montaigne's observation that each of us calls barbarous whatever is not our own custom anticipates Haidt's journey out of his own moral matrix in Orissa.
recap:
Imagine a clever young liberal from a comfortable New York suburb, quietly sure that the people on the other side of politics are mostly wrong, and possibly a bit wicked. That is Jonathan Haidt in the nineteen eighties. He studies philosophy, which seems to say that morality is mainly careful reasoning. He is not convinced, and he turns to psychology instead.

In Philadelphia he tells people strange little stories. A family eats their dog after it is killed by a car. Nobody is harmed. Is it wrong? Most people say yes, and when every reason they offer is ruled out, they still say yes. They know it is wrong. They just cannot say why.

Then he spends three months in India, in a world of duty, deference and purity that at first feels alien. Slowly he begins to see it from the inside, and he comes home curious, for the first time, about the people he had dismissed. Nearly twenty years later he publishes The Righteous Mind.

Its first big idea is the elephant and the rider. The elephant is intuition, fast and powerful. The rider is reasoning, and it is less a driver than a press secretary, explaining whatever the elephant has already decided. If you want to change a mind, you speak to the elephant first, with respect, relationship and story.

The second idea is that morality is like a tongue with several taste receptors: care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and liberty. In his surveys, American liberals lean mainly on care and fairness. Conservatives use all of them more evenly. Even fairness tastes different: equality for one side, getting what you deserve for the other.

The third idea is that we are, in his phrase, ninety per cent chimp and ten per cent bee. Mostly selfish, but able to flip a hive switch and lose ourselves in a team, a ritual or a cause. Morality binds us together, and it also blinds us to outsiders.

The fourth is a humbling test. Asked to predict how the other side would answer, liberals did worst at understanding conservatives.

The fifth is a caution. Critics argue that reasoning matters more than Haidt allows, that harm may lie underneath most moral judgements, and that the evolutionary story about groups is unproven.

Haidt did not end up a convert. He ended up someone who could see why decent people disagree. So the next time you meet someone who seems impossible to persuade, assume they are tasting a different flavour, not that they are stupid. Here is the line to remember: build the relationship before the argument, because the rider follows the elephant.
